```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 150, out.width = "100%")
```

An APC of -2% per year means little without its confidence interval, and
the interval depends on assumptions about the errors: is every year equally
precise, are neighboring years independent, and is the location of the
joinpoint itself uncertain? This vignette analyzes influenza and pneumonia
mortality, whose 1918 pandemic peak and the arrival of antibiotics make it a
demanding series, under different error models and shows how the
conclusions move.

```{r}
library(joinpoint)
library(ggplot2)
flu <- subset(us_mortality, cause == "Influenza and Pneumonia")
```

## Weights: which years are precise?

With **constant variance** every year counts equally. When each value comes
with a standard error, or is calculated from counts, the fit is weighted by
the inverse variance; on the log scale the variance of a rate is
approximately its squared standard error divided by the squared rate (the
delta method), and a count of `c` events gets weight `c`. Weights matter
when precision changes over time, for example when a population grows
severalfold over the study period or a disease becomes rare. When the
denominators are similar every year, as for the prevalence of obesity class
III in `ontario_bmi`, weighted and unweighted fits agree:

```{r}
ob <- subset(ontario_bmi, category == "Obesity class III")
weighted <- joinpoint(ob, year, count = count, population = births,
                      type = "percent", kmax = 2, method = "bic",
                      ci_method = "parametric")
unweighted <- joinpoint(ob, year, count = count, population = births,
                        type = "percent", variance = "constant", kmax = 2,
                        method = "bic", ci_method = "parametric")
data.frame(jp_table(weighted)[, 1:2], weighted = jp_table(weighted)[, 3],
           unweighted = jp_table(unweighted)[, 3])
```

## Two kinds of confidence interval

The **parametric** intervals treat the joinpoints as known. An APC interval
uses t quantiles with the standard error from separate regressions of the
segments; an AAPC interval uses normal quantiles, or t quantiles when its
range lies inside one segment; and the interval of a joinpoint location
collects the candidate locations whose best fit is close enough to the
overall best (Lerman 1980).
Simulations showed that they are too wide for the AAPC (Kim et al. 2017)
and can be too narrow for short segments (Kim et al. 2022). The **empirical quantile** method,
the package default, resamples the residuals, refits the whole model
including the joinpoint locations 5001 times, and takes percentiles. It
therefore reflects the uncertainty about where the trend changed.

```{r}
fit_par <- joinpoint(flu, year, rate, kmax = 3, ci_method = "parametric")
fit_eq <- joinpoint(flu, year, rate, kmax = 3)
cmp <- merge(
  apc(fit_par)[, c("segment", "estimate", "lower", "upper")],
  apc(fit_eq)[, c("segment", "lower", "upper")],
  by = "segment", suffixes = c("_parametric", "_empirical")
)
cmp$width_ratio <- (cmp$upper_empirical - cmp$lower_empirical) /
  (cmp$upper_parametric - cmp$lower_parametric)
cmp
```

Every empirical interval is wider here. For the short 1936 to 1950 segment
it is more than three times as wide and strongly asymmetric: if the two
joinpoints move closer together the segment becomes much steeper, and the
parametric interval ignores this. Part of the extra width is by design: the
resampled residuals are drawn from a smoothed version of their empirical
distribution whose tails extend beyond the observed residuals. The fitted
curve band and the joinpoint intervals show the same uncertainty on the
data scale:

```{r, fig.alt = "Influenza and pneumonia death rate by year on a logarithmic axis with the fitted joinpoint model, the 95% empirical quantile band of the fitted curve and the confidence intervals of the joinpoint locations."}
autoplot(fit_eq, joinpoint_ci = TRUE, log_y = TRUE)
```

## Autocorrelated errors

Mortality in adjacent years shares unmeasured influences, so errors may be
positively autocorrelated. The autocorrelation function of the residuals
shows whether this is plausible:

```{r, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Autocorrelation function of the standardized residuals of the influenza and pneumonia model."}
plot_residuals(fit_par, type = "acf")
```

A first order autocorrelation can be estimated from the residuals of the
model with the most joinpoints, but Kim et al. (2000) found that the
correction costs much power to detect joinpoints: a joinpoint and an
autocorrelated wiggle are hard to tell apart. A sensitivity analysis over
plausible values is more informative:

```{r}
sens <- lapply(c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3), function(r) {
  f <- joinpoint(flu, year, rate, kmax = 3, autocorrelation = r,
                 ci_method = "parametric")
  data.frame(rho = r, joinpoints = toString(joinpoints(f)$estimate),
             aapc = aapc(f)$estimate, lower = aapc(f)$lower,
             upper = aapc(f)$upper)
})
do.call(rbind, sens)
```

The joinpoints and the AAPC barely move, and the interval widens slowly
with the assumed autocorrelation: the conclusions do not hinge on the
independence assumption.

## References

Kim HJ, Fay MP, Feuer EJ, Midthune DN (2000). Permutation tests for
joinpoint regression with applications to cancer rates. *Statistics in
Medicine* 19:335-351.

Kim HJ, Luo J, Chen HS, Green D, Buckman D, Byrne J, Feuer EJ (2017).
Improved confidence interval for average annual percent change in trend
analysis. *Statistics in Medicine* 36:3059-3074.

Kim HJ, Chen HS, Byrne J, Wheeler B, Feuer EJ (2022). Twenty years since
Joinpoint 1.0: two major enhancements, their justification, and impact.
*Statistics in Medicine* 41:3102-3130.

Lerman PM (1980). Fitting segmented regression models by grid search.
*Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C* 29:77-84.
